newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australians switch to food from shopping - survey.
newsitem.headline: Australians switch to food from shopping - survey.

text.p: Australian consumers aiming to break the shackles of the early-1990s recession are switching their discretionary spending from retail stores to restaurants and movie theatres, a new survey released on Monday has found.

Advertising agency George Patterson Bates and research centre The Values Bank released the inaugural George Patterson Bates Values Bank quarterly survey of spending patterns and behaviour, showing that discretionary purchases in retail stores had fallen about 12 percent in the last nine months.
But spending on entertainment rose 12 percent and spending on food in restaurants and cafes rose 10 percent in that period.
The survey is compiled from interviews with 1,100 consumers drawn from a pool of 60,000 interviewed by the Roy Morgan Research centre.

"After a long period of hibernation during the recession and the cautious years following it, consumers are now once again enjoying that liberating feeling of spending," Values Bank Managing Director Ross Honeywill said.
"But significantly, this spend trend is centred on the need to reward ourselves -- it is about instant personal gratification," Honeywill said in a statement.
The survey found that up to a quarter of the fall in retail activity was due to extra entertainment spending.
The top-earning four percent of the population were leading the food and entertainment spending spree, it found.
"A quarter of all consumers are committed to consuming experiences and not products," George Patterson Bates managing director Ian Smith said.
The survey also found that only a third of those who can afford to invest or save actually do so.
The survey's index of spending on food rose from about 103 to about 107 in the March quarter, while the total non-food retail purchase index fell to 88 from 105 in the quarter.
The trend in non-food retail purchases has fallen steadily through 1996 and is forecast to fall further in the June quarter.
